'''''Thunbergia alata''''', commonly called '''black-eyed Susan vine''',<ref name="PA"/> is a herbaceous perennial climbing plant species in the family [[Acanthaceae]].  It is native to [[Eastern Africa]], and has been naturalized in other parts of the world.

It is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] in gardens and in hanging baskets.  The name 'Black-eyed Susan' is thought to have come from a character that figures in many traditional ballads and songs.  In the ''Ballad of Black-eyed Susan'' by [[John Gay]], Susan goes aboard a ship in-dock to ask the sailors where her lover [[Dianthus barbatus|Sweet William]] has gone.  Black-eyed Susan is also a name given to other species of flowers in the genus ''[[Rudbeckia]]''.

==Description==
[[File:Black-eyed_Susan_1.jpg|thumb|220px|Flowers|left]]
''Thunbergia alata'' has a vine habit, and can grow to a height of {{convert|5|m|ft}} high in warmer zones,<ref>[https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/thunbergia_alata.htm Thunbergia alata Bojer ex Sims] Weeds of Australia</ref> or much less as a container plant or as an annual. It has twining stems with heart or arrow-shaped leaves. The three and a half to seven and a half centimeters long and two and a half centimeters wide leaves are triangular to heart-shaped. Their edges are wavy and both surfaces are hairy. The [[leaf blade]]s sit on up to six and a half centimeters long [[petiole (botany)|petioles]], which attach at a distance of four and a half to 13 centimeters on the one to one and a quarter millimeter thick stem axis.

===Inflorescence===
The hairy, mostly orange-yellow flowers have five petals and appear throughout the growing season, which grow on up to eight and a half centimeters long [[inflorescence]] axes. They typically are warm orange with a characteristic dark spot in the centre. The central two centimeter long [[corolla (botany)|corolla]] tube is black-violet. Each of the single flowers has two triangular to oval, hairy [[bract]]s that taper towards the outside. They are 18 to 20 millimeters long and nine to ten millimeters wide. The serrated [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]] is about two millimeters long and has between 15 and 17 awl-shaped lobes. The corolla tube measures around four centimeters and shows five two centimeter large corolla lobes with right-hand covering [[buds]] on the outside.<ref name="PA">{{Cite web|url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/|title=PlantZAfrica.com Homepage|website=www.plantzafrica.com}}</ref>

The plant flowers from mid-summer to the first frost, but it will flower all year round in milder, frostless climate zones.<ref>[https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=thunbergia~alata  Thunbergia alata Bojer ex Sims] PlantNET</ref><ref>[https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/black-eyed-susan-vine-thunbergia-alata/#:~:text=Plants%20bloom%20from%20mid%2Dsummer,pastels%20and%20white%20as%20well. Black-eyed Susan Vine, Thunbergia alata] [[University of Wisconsin]]-Madison Division of Extension</ref>

The 16 to 18 millimeter long fruits are finely hairy. At the base they have a diameter of seven millimeters. The four seeds measure 3.5 millimeters.

==Cultivation==
''Thunbergia alata'' seed is easy to germinate in humus-rich soil with some sand and it can be grown from [[cuttings (plants)|cuttings]]. Soaking the seeds in a dish of warm water over night will help improve seed germination when planted. It is a fast grower, blooming quickly, with light trimming encouraging more blossoms.<ref name="PA" />  There are cultivars with red, orange, red-orange, white, pale yellow, or bright yellow flowers, with or without the characteristic chocolate-purple centre which inspires the common name.

==Distribution==
The plant is originally from East Africa, and has almost a world distribution including tropical and subtropical areas like China, eastern [[Australia]], [[Hawaii]], [[Southern US]] in the states of [[Texas]] and [[Florida]],<ref name=autogenerated2>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/ClassificationServlet?source=profile&symbol=THAL3&display=63|title=Classification - USDA PLANTS|website=Plants USDA Gov}}</ref> Colombia, [[Puerto Rico]],<ref name="Mutt and Rivera">{{cite web |last1=Mari Mutt |first1=José A. |last2=Almodóvar Rivera |first2=José R. |title=Animales y plantas con historias |url=http://www.edicionesdigitales.info/imagenes/imagenes.pdf |website=Ediciones Digitales |publisher=University of Mayaguez |language=Spanish}}</ref> Mexico, South Africa, Portugal, Japan, New Zealand, [[Cerrado]] [[vegetation]] of [[Brazil]], Argentina, Madagascar, India, Thailand and Philippines, among others.

It is used all around the world as a garden plant, but has managed to "[[escaped plant|escape]]" to the wilderness, naturalizing in tropical and temperate forests. It has been widely reported as [[Invasive species]], especially in the [[Caribbean]] and [[Pacific islands]], from Mexico to Colombia, and in Japan,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.conabio.gob.mx/malezasdemexico/acanthaceae/thunbergia-alata/fichas/ficha.htm|title=Thunbergia alata - ficha informativa|website=www.conabio.gob.mx}}</ref> due to the fast growing of the plant; the ease of wild [[pollination]] during sporadic flowering times; its vine-growing strategies that strangle or create shadow on other plants; its difficulty to eradicate by hand (as it leaves underground rhizomes that rapidly grow back); its lack of usual [[predator]]s in non native regions; plus, people who are unaware of its harmful nature to other plants in the wilderness tend to admire its beauty and might opt not to remove it.<ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/53646#tobiologyAndEcology| title = Thunbergia alata (black eyed Susan)}}</ref>
